title: 第266章 审判之焰血拓第265章 审判之焰空名者
slug: 黯潮纪元异世界的崛起
lines: 审判之焰贴地砖蔓延到陈默膝前时，他闻到了自己的焦味。
不是衣服在烧。是眉毛被热浪烤卷的味道，混着皮甲表面油脂受热后渗出的酸气。火焰距他膝盖不到半米，却没有直接烧上来，而是像水碰到油一样，沿着空剑霜痕的边缘绕开，在霜痕两侧烧出两条平行的火线。
火线在他身后汇合，把他圈在里面。
陈默盯着那些火焰——它们不是要烧死他。火舌从地面卷起时，方向是一致的，全部指向盔甲胸口那个缺口，像箭头。火焰每次靠近空剑霜痕都会短暂停顿，火苗矮下去半寸，像在等某个音节被念出来。
“你在催我。”陈默说。
声音在火里被吞掉了。没有回声。
他低头看膝前的空剑。剑脊上的霜痕已经渗进金属表面，不是浮冰，是凹进去的阴文——笔画不像任何埃尔德兰文字，但结构他见过。三星堆青铜器上被磨掉的铭文，石锤在表面敲出的凹坑，墨拓上去就是反写的字。
血还在往霜痕里渗。
他抬起右手，掌心的伤口结了薄薄一层血痂，手指一握，痂就裂开，血重新渗出来。他盯着那些血看了三秒，然后把整只手掌按在剑脊上。
霜没化。
血被吸进凹痕里，像墨汁灌进刻好的槽道，沿着阴文的笔画一分一分地扩散。那些原本模糊的凹痕在血渗入后变得清晰，笔画边缘像刀切一样整齐，每一条线都带着锋利的转折。
陈默把掌心抬起来。
剑脊上留下一个暗红色的手印。手印的纹路和阴文叠在一起，在血色的填充下，那些笔画终于变得可辨——不是冰晶，不是埃尔德兰的符文，是刻在金属上的母模，像印章的阴面。
他眯起眼，侧过头，让审判之焰的火光从侧面打在剑脊上。阴影让那些笔画更深了，血色的凹痕在火光里像燃烧的沟渠。
第一组可辨音节出现在剑脊中段。
陈默的脊椎窜过一阵冷。不是恐惧，是考古学家的本能——他在三星堆的青铜器上拓过太多类似的铭文，那些笔画的结构、转折的角度、收尾时的顿笔，一模一样。
“这是中国的东西。”他说。
声音在火里闷掉了。
他跪在地上，把空剑横在膝前，用左手按住剑尖，右手的食指和中指并拢，沿着血渗出的凹痕描过去。
手在抖。
不是怕。是那些笔画太熟悉了，熟悉到他不愿意承认自己认出了它们。他的指尖划过第一组笔画——一个向右倾斜的短横，一个向下转折的竖，一个向左回勾的尾。不是埃尔德兰的字母排列，是汉字的结构。
“陈”字的古音转写。
他盯着那组笔画，脑子里闪过三星堆的青铜尊，尊内壁的铭文，那些被磨掉的名字。考古报告里写的是“磨损严重，不可辨识”，但他见过实物，见过石锤在铭文表面留下的敲击痕迹——不是自然磨损，是故意磨掉的。
有人不想让那些名字留下来。
审判之焰在他身后跳了一下。火舌从地面卷起半米高，又压下去，像在催促。
陈默深吸一口气，把手指按在第二组笔画上。这组笔画更密，横和竖叠在一起，像某种古老的封泥印文。他描了三次才确认——不是汉字，是音节的转写，把发音转成笔画结构的文字系统，像西夏文，像女真文，像所有被历史磨掉一半的文字。
“第三姓名系统。”他低声说。
盔甲没有回应。
陈默的手指停在第三组笔画上。这组笔画比前两组浅，血渗进去的速度也慢，像凹槽刻得不够深，或者刻好后被人刮过一遍。他把掌心的血挤出来，重新按在剑脊上，用力压下去，让血渗进那些浅的凹槽里。
第三组笔画开始显现。
不是名字。是一个数字序列，和盔甲念过的契约编号前段一模一样——瑟兰迪尔·第三纪元·第十三序列·第七星阶——但后面多了两行。两行不属于埃尔德兰纪年的数字。
第二行：四川。
陈默的手指僵在剑脊上。
1987。四川。他在三星堆遗址出生的年份，他在坑边学会走路的省份。那些数字和地名不是刻上去的，是被磨掉后又从另一面渗出来的，像有人用橡皮擦掉了一行铅笔字，但纸张上留下的压痕还在。
“不是巧合。”他说。
声音在火里碎掉了。

When the flames of judgment spread against the floor tiles and reached Chen Mo's knees, he smelled his own burnt smell.
It's not the clothes that are burning. It's the smell of eyebrows being curled by heat waves, mixed with the sour smell that oozes from the heated oil on the surface of leather nails. The flame was less than half a meter away from his knees, but it did not burn directly. Instead, like water touching oil, it circled along the edge of the frost mark on the empty sword, burning two parallel lines of fire on both sides of the frost mark.
The lines of fire converged behind him, trapping him inside.
Chen Mo stared at the flames - they were not trying to burn him to death. When the tongues of fire rolled up from the ground, they all pointed in the same direction, pointing toward the gap on the chest of the armor, like arrows. Every time the flame comes close to the frost mark of the empty sword, it will pause briefly, and the flame will drop half an inch, as if it is waiting for a certain syllable to be pronounced.
"You're urging me." Chen Mo said.
The sound was swallowed up in the fire. No echo.
He looked down at the empty sword in front of his knees. The frost marks on the spine of the sword have penetrated into the metal surface. They are not ice floes, but indented inscriptions - the strokes are not like any Eldran writing, but the structure is something he has seen before. The inscriptions that have been worn away on the Sanxingdui bronzes, the pits made by stone hammers on the surface, and the ink rubbings on them are the words written backwards.
Blood is still seeping into the frost marks.
He raised his right hand, and the wound on his palm was covered with a thin layer of blood scab. When he touched it with his fingers, the scab cracked and blood seeped out again. He stared at the blood for three seconds, and then pressed his entire palm on the spine of the sword.
The frost has not melted.
The blood was sucked into the dents, like ink pouring into the carved channels, spreading along the strokes of the inscription. The originally blurry dents became clear after the blood seeped into them. The edges of the strokes were as neat as knife cuts, and each line had a sharp twist.
Chen Mo raised his palm.
A dark red handprint was left on the sword spine. The lines of the handprint and the inscriptions were overlapped, and with the blood filling, those strokes finally became discernible—not ice crystals, not Eldran's runes, but the mother mold engraved on the metal, like the negative side of a seal.
He narrowed his eyes and turned his head, letting the flames of the flame of judgment hit the sword spine from the side. The shadows made the strokes darker, and the bloody dents looked like burning ditches in the firelight.
The first set of discernible syllables appears in the middle of the spine of the sword.
A chill ran down Chen Mo's spine. It's not fear, it's the instinct of an archaeologist - he has carved too many similar inscriptions on the bronzes in Sanxingdui, and the structure of the strokes, the angle of the turn, and the pause at the end are exactly the same.
"This is a Chinese thing," he said.
The sound was muffled in the fire.
***
He knelt on the ground, held the empty sword in front of his knees, held the tip of the sword with his left hand, put the index and middle fingers of his right hand together and traced the dent where the blood seeped out.
Hands shaking.
Not afraid. Those strokes were so familiar that he didn't want to admit that he recognized them. His fingertips traced the first set of strokes - a short horizontal line tilting to the right, a vertical line turning downward, and a tail hooking back to the left. It's not the arrangement of letters in Eldran, it's the structure of Chinese characters.
The ancient pronunciation of the word "Chen".
He stared at the set of strokes, and the bronze statue of Sanxingdui, the inscriptions on the inner wall of the statue, and the erased names flashed through his mind. The archaeological report stated that it was "severely worn and unrecognizable," but he had seen the actual object and the impact marks left by stone hammers on the surface of the inscription - not natural wear, but deliberate wear.
Someone didn't want those names to stick around.
The Flame of Judgment jumped behind him. The tongues of fire rose half a meter high from the ground, then pressed down again, as if urging.
Chen Mo took a deep breath and pressed his fingers on the second set of strokes. This group of strokes is denser, stacked horizontally and vertically, like some kind of ancient mud seal. He traced it three times before confirming it - it was not Chinese characters, but a transliteration of syllables, a writing system that converts pronunciation into stroke structure, like Xixia script, like Jurchen script, and like all scripts that have been half worn away by history.
"Third name system," he whispered.
The armor didn't respond.
Chen Mo's fingers stopped on the third set of strokes. This group of strokes is shallower than the previous two groups, and the blood seeps in more slowly, as if the grooves were not deep enough, or someone scratched them after they were carved. He squeezed the blood out of his palm, pressed it on the spine of the sword again, and pressed it down hard, letting the blood seep into the shallow grooves.
A third set of strokes begins to appear.
Not a name. It is a sequence of numbers that is exactly the same as the first part of the contract number read by the armor - Thranduil·Third Age·Thirteenth Sequence·Seventh Star Level-but there are two more lines at the end. Two lines of numbers that do not belong to the Elderan chronology.
First row: 1987.
Second row: Sichuan.
Chen Mo's fingers were frozen on the sword spine.
1987. Sichuan. The year he was born in the Sanxingdui ruins, the province where he learned to walk by the pit. The numbers and place names were not engraved on them. They were rubbed off and then seeped out from the other side. It was like someone had erased a line of pencil writing with an eraser, but the indentation left on the paper was still there.
"It's not a coincidence," he said.
The sound was shattered in the fire.
